course.title: Python
course.description: A research-driven, beginner-to-advanced Python course that develops language fluency, problem-solving ability, maintainable application design, testing, packaging, data persistence, concurrency, and security-aware programming. It starts with Python fundamentals and progresses through the standard library, object-oriented and protocol-oriented design, typed APIs, project environments, testing and performance, concurrent execution, secure coding, and a complete standard-library capstone. The course is appropriate for learners who can use a computer comfortably and want a serious practical command of Python itself rather than a framework-specific career track.
prerequisites: Basic computer literacy and ability to work with files and folders.
Comfort using a text editor or IDE.
No prior Python programming experience is required.
learningOutcomes: Write, read, debug, and refactor idiomatic Python programs using core language constructs and built-in data structures.
Design reusable functions, modules, packages, classes, protocols, and typed APIs with clear contracts.
Use Python standard-library tools for files, paths, serialization, databases, command-line programs, logging, testing, and configuration.
Create and maintain isolated Python environments and modern project metadata with `venv`, pip, and `pyproject.toml`.
Build testable applications and use tracebacks, breakpoints, logging, and measurement to diagnose and improve them.
Choose appropriate concurrency models for I/O-bound and CPU-bound work using threads, processes, executors, and asyncio.
Apply security-aware Python practices including input validation, parameterized SQL, safe subprocess invocation, secret handling, and careful logging.
Plan, implement, test, package, and explain a multi-file Python application using professional engineering boundaries.

modules.title: Python Foundations and Execution
modules.description: Build a reliable mental model of Python execution, values, variables, expressions, control flow, and the development workflow.

lessons.title: Python, the Interpreter, and Program Execution
lessons.description: Understand what Python code is, how the interpreter executes it, and how scripts differ from interactive use.
learningObjectives: Explain the roles of source code, the Python interpreter, and the standard library.
Run a script from the command line and inspect the active interpreter.
Distinguish syntax errors from runtime exceptions at a basic level.

notes.text: A usable mental model

Python source is parsed and compiled to bytecode before execution by a Python implementation such as CPython. The language defines semantics, while implementation details such as bytecode layout are implementation-specific.

print("hello")
name = input("Name: ")
print(f"Hello, {name}!")

items: Use `python --version` or `python3 --version` to identify the interpreter being invoked.
Prefer running the file you intend to execute rather than relying on an IDE setting whose interpreter may differ.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the Python standard library?
options: A collection of modules distributed with Python
A web framework included with Python
quiz.answer: A collection of modules distributed with Python
quiz.explanation: The standard library supplies modules for common programming and system tasks; it is distributed with Python rather than being a separate web framework or database engine.

summary: Python programs are source files executed by a Python implementation.
Interactive prompts are excellent for quick experiments; scripts and modules are better for repeatable programs.

lessons.title: Variables, Objects, and Core Data Types
lessons.description: Learn how names refer to objects and how Python’s primary built-in types behave.
learningObjectives: Explain names, objects, identity, and equality.
Use integers, floats, booleans, strings, None, lists, tuples, sets, and dictionaries appropriately.
Choose a data type based on mutability and required operations.

notes.text: Names point to objects
Assignment binds a name to an object; it does not copy the object by default. Equality (`==`) compares values, while identity (`is`) checks whether two references point to the same object.

items = ["a", "b"]
alias = items
copy = items.copy()
alias.append("c")
print(items)   # alias sees the same list
print(copy)    # independent shallow copy

items: Lists, dictionaries, and sets are mutable. Tuples and strings are immutable.
Use `is None` for the singleton `None`; do not use `== None`.

quiz.question: What does `a is b` test?
quiz.answer: Object identity
quiz.explanation: The `is` operator tests whether two expressions refer to the same object.

summary: Python variable assignment binds names to objects rather than declaring fixed storage types.
Mutability determines whether an object can change after creation.

lessons.title: Expressions, Operators, and Truthiness
lessons.description: Use arithmetic, comparison, boolean, membership, and conditional expressions precisely.
learningObjectives: Evaluate precedence and grouping in expressions.
Use short-circuit boolean evaluation intentionally.
Explain truthy and falsy values in conditional contexts.

notes.text:
score = 74
passed = score >= 50 and score <= 100
print(passed)

value = []
if not value:
    print("empty")
`and` and `or` return one of their operands, not necessarily a boolean. This is useful for defaulting and guard expressions but should be used only when it remains readable.
Avoid clever boolean expressions when an explicit `if` makes the intent clearer, especially when `None` and empty containers have different meanings.

quiz.question: What is the safest way to test that `value` is `None`?
quiz.answer: value is None
quiz.explanation: `None` is a singleton used to represent the absence of a value, and identity comparison is the conventional and correct test.

summary: Operator precedence affects the order in which expressions are evaluated.
Truthiness lets many values be used directly in conditions, but `None` and an empty container can represent different business states.

lessons.title: Control Flow: Conditions, Loops, and Pattern Matching
lessons.description: Control the execution path of programs with conditional statements and iteration.
learningObjectives: Write multi-branch conditionals.
Use `for`, `while`, `break`, `continue`, and loop `else` correctly.
Use structural pattern matching for suitable fixed-shape cases.

notes.text: Iteration is data-driven
Python `for` loops iterate over an iterable rather than requiring an index counter. Use `enumerate()` when the index is actually needed.

def describe(value):
    match value:
        case {"kind": "error", "code": code}:
            return f"error {code}"
        case {"kind": "ok", "value": value}:
            return f"ok {value}"
        case _:
            return "unknown"

items: Pattern matching is useful for structured data, not as a replacement for every `if` statement.
A loop `else` clause runs when the loop completes without hitting `break`.

quiz.question: When does the `else` block of a `for` loop execute?
quiz.answer: When the loop finishes without `break`
quiz.explanation: The loop `else` executes only if normal iteration reaches completion without encountering `break`.

summary: Prefer direct iteration over manual indexing.
Use pattern matching when the shape of the data is central to the branching logic.

lessons.title: Practical: Build a Command-Line Expense Calculator
lessons.description: Turn the foundational syntax into a small program that parses repeated user input and produces a useful result.
learningObjectives: Validate numeric input with exceptions.
Accumulate values using a loop.
Format a final report for a user.

notes.text: Implementation pattern
A small CLI program should separate input collection from the calculation so the calculation can later be tested independently.

items: Keep validation close to the boundary where untrusted text enters the program.
Prefer functions with explicit inputs and outputs over hidden global state.

practicals.title: Expense Calculator
practicals.description: Build a loop-based CLI that accepts expense amounts until the user enters `done`, rejects negative or malformed amounts, and prints the count and total.
steps: Create `parse_amount()` to convert and validate one amount.
Read input repeatedly until the sentinel `done` is entered.
Catch `ValueError` and continue without terminating the program.
Print the number of accepted entries and their total to two decimal places.
practicals.output: For valid entries the program reports the count and total. Invalid input prints a validation message and the loop continues.

quiz.question: Why should numeric conversion errors be handled explicitly in a CLI?
options: Because user input is always trusted
Because conversion can raise an exception
quiz.answer: Because conversion can raise an exception
quiz.explanation: `float()` may raise `ValueError` when input cannot be interpreted as a number, so a CLI should handle that failure rather than crash.

summary: The exercise combines input, loops, validation, and formatting.
The same validation function can be reused by a larger application.

tasks.title: Grade Classification Function
tasks.description: Implement a pure function that classifies a numeric score into a named grade band.
tasks.problemStatement: The function receives a numeric score from 0 through 100 and must reject values outside that interval. Return `A`, `B`, `C`, `D`, or `F` using clearly defined thresholds.
tasks.hint: Validate the range before classifying so boundary values cannot silently fall into an unintended branch.
tasks.solutionExplanation: Validation isolates the domain error. Conditions descend from the highest threshold so each score matches exactly one branch.

modules.description: Master collections, slicing, comprehensions, unpacking, iterables, and transformations that make Python code concise without making it cryptic.

lessons.title: Strings and Text Processing
lessons.description: Work safely with Unicode text, slicing, formatting, and common string operations.
learningObjectives: Use slicing and string methods for transformations.
Explain why Python strings are Unicode text objects.
Format data with f-strings while separating formatting from logic.

notes.text:
name = "Ada Lovelace"
first, last = name.split()
print(f"{last}, {first}")

message = "  Python  "
print(message.strip().lower())

items: Strings are immutable; methods return new strings rather than editing the original in place.
Prefer explicit encodings at I/O boundaries; internally, Python `str` represents Unicode text.

quiz.question: What does `"-".join(["a", "b"])` produce?
quiz.answer: a-b
quiz.explanation: `join` inserts the separator between elements of an iterable of strings.

summary: String methods provide composable operations such as `split`, `join`, `replace`, `strip`, and `casefold`.
F-strings are for presentation and are not a substitute for validation or localization design.

lessons.title: Lists, Tuples, Sets, and Dictionaries
lessons.description: Choose and combine Python’s primary collection types based on ordering, uniqueness, key lookup, and mutability.
learningObjectives: Use list mutation and slicing correctly.
Use sets for membership and uniqueness.
Use dictionaries for keyed data and safe lookup patterns.

items: Dictionary keys must be hashable objects.
Use `.get()` when absence is expected and a default value is meaningful; use indexing when missing keys are exceptional.

quiz.question: Which structure is best suited to map a username to a role?
quiz.answer: dict
quiz.explanation: A dictionary directly models key-to-value association and provides keyed lookup.

summary: Different collections encode different invariants.
Set membership is the natural choice for uniqueness and membership checks; dictionaries model keyed records.

lessons.title: Comprehensions, Unpacking, and Generator Expressions
lessons.description: Use comprehensions and unpacking to express transformations clearly and understand when generators save memory.
learningObjectives: Write list, set, and dictionary comprehensions.
Use iterable unpacking in assignments and function calls.
Explain the lazy behavior of generator expressions.

notes.text:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]
squares = [n * n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0]
lookup = {n: n * n for n in numbers}
print(squares, lookup)

first, *middle, last = [10, 20, 30, 40]
print(first, middle, last)
A generator expression produces values on demand. This is useful for large streams because it avoids materializing every transformed value at once.

quiz.question: Why can a generator expression use less memory than a list comprehension?
options: It stores values lazily instead of building the whole list
It uses a different integer type
quiz.answer: It stores values lazily instead of building the whole list
quiz.explanation: A generator yields items as requested rather than constructing and retaining the full result at creation time.

summary: Comprehensions are ideal for simple one-step transformations with understandable predicates.
Switch to named loops or functions when comprehension logic becomes difficult to read.

lessons.title: Iterators, `enumerate`, `zip`, and Data Pipelines
lessons.description: Understand the iterator protocol and build readable multi-stage transformations.
learningObjectives: Distinguish iterables from iterators.
Use `enumerate` and `zip` correctly.
Compose transformations while preserving readability.

notes.text:
names = ["Asha", "Ben", "Chen"]
scores = [84, 91, 77]
for name, score in zip(names, scores):
    print(name, score)
`iter(obj)` asks an object for an iterator; `next(iterator)` advances it. A `for` loop manages these calls for you and catches `StopIteration`.

quiz.question: What happens when `zip(a, b)` receives sequences of different lengths?
options: It stops when the shortest input is exhausted
quiz.answer: It stops when the shortest input is exhausted
quiz.explanation: Standard `zip` terminates when the shortest iterable is exhausted.

summary: Python’s iteration protocol is based on `__iter__` and `__next__`.
`zip` stops at the shortest input by default; use explicit length checks when truncation would hide a bug.

lessons.title: Useful Standard-Library Collections and Algorithms
lessons.description: Use `collections`, `itertools`, and `functools` to solve common data-processing problems without reinventing them.
learningObjectives: Use `Counter`, `defaultdict`, and `deque` appropriately.
Use `itertools` for composable iterator operations.
Use `functools` utilities such as `lru_cache` and `partial` where they clarify design.

notes.text:
from collections import Counter, deque

counts = Counter("banana")
queue = deque(["job-1", "job-2"])
queue.append("job-3")
print(counts["a"])
print(queue.popleft())
Memoization can trade memory for speed. Cache only when repeated inputs and stable results make the trade worthwhile.

quiz.question: Which type is designed for efficient insertion/removal from both ends?
quiz.answer: deque
quiz.explanation: `collections.deque` is designed for efficient appends and pops from both ends.

summary: The standard library contains specialized containers and iterator building blocks.
Caching is a design decision, not an automatic optimization.

lessons.description: Process a stream of structured records with grouping, counting, and stable output.
learningObjectives: Aggregate records with dictionaries and counters.
Sort results using a key function.
Build output data without mutating the source records.

notes.text:
records = [
    {"service": "api", "status": 200},
    {"service": "api", "status": 500},
    {"service": "worker", "status": 200},
]

items: Separate ingestion, aggregation, and formatting so each stage has one job.
Use stable sort keys and explicit reverse flags when deterministic output matters.

quiz.question: Which standard type is a natural fit for counting status codes?
quiz.answer: Counter
quiz.explanation: `collections.Counter` is specialized for tallying hashable values.

summary: Aggregation is easier to reason about when raw records remain unchanged.
Sorting should be performed on the final derived structure, not repeatedly during ingestion.

lessons.title: Data Modeling with `dataclass`
lessons.description: Create explicit domain objects with readable representations and controlled defaults.
learningObjectives: Define a dataclass with typed fields.
Understand default values and `default_factory`.
Choose dataclasses instead of unstructured dictionaries when a stable domain model improves correctness.

notes.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Job:
    name: str
    retries: int = 0
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

job = Job("index", tags=["nightly"])
print(job)
Never use a mutable object such as `[]` directly as a field default. Use `default_factory` to create a new list for each instance.

quiz.question: Why is `default_factory=list` used for a mutable dataclass field?
options: To create a separate list for each instance
To convert it to a tuple
quiz.answer: To create a separate list for each instance
quiz.explanation: `default_factory` creates a fresh object for each dataclass instance, preventing accidental sharing of mutable state.

summary: Dataclasses provide generated methods for common record-like classes.
Typed fields communicate intent but are not runtime validation rules by themselves.

objectives: Use dictionaries and sets to enforce uniqueness.

modules.title: Functions, Scope, Exceptions, and Resource Safety
modules.description: Design reusable functions, understand scope and closures, handle failures intentionally, and manage resources safely.

lessons.title: Functions, Parameters, Return Values, and Docstrings
lessons.description: Design functions that communicate their contracts clearly.
learningObjectives: Use positional-only, keyword-only, default, and variadic parameters appropriately.
Return values instead of relying on hidden state.
Write useful docstrings for public behavior.

items: A keyword-only parameter can make calls self-documenting.
Avoid default mutable arguments such as `items=[]`; evaluate defaults once at function definition time.

quiz.question: When is a keyword-only parameter useful?
options: When you want to require an argument be passed by name
quiz.answer: When you want to require an argument be passed by name
quiz.explanation: Keyword-only parameters make invocation explicit and can prevent accidental positional swapping.

summary: Functions should expose a small, explicit contract.
Default arguments are evaluated once when the function is defined, which is why mutable defaults are risky.

lessons.title: Scope, Closures, and `global`/`nonlocal`
lessons.description: Understand LEGB lookup and how nested functions capture surrounding state.
learningObjectives: Trace name resolution using local, enclosing, global, and built-in scopes.
Create closures intentionally.
Explain when `nonlocal` is appropriate.

notes.text:
def make_counter():
    count = 0
    def increment():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    return increment

counter = make_counter()
print(counter())
print(counter())
Closures are powerful, but excessive hidden mutable state can make code harder to test. Prefer explicit objects or function parameters when the state should be visible to callers.

quiz.question: Which keyword lets a nested function rebind a variable in an enclosing function scope?
quiz.answer: nonlocal
quiz.explanation: `nonlocal` targets a binding in the nearest enclosing function scope.

summary: Python resolves names using local, enclosing, global, then built-in scopes.
A closure retains access to variables from its defining lexical scope after the outer function returns.

lessons.title: Exceptions as Control Flow for Failure
lessons.description: Raise, catch, chain, and design exceptions to make failure modes explicit.
learningObjectives: Differentiate `try`, `except`, `else`, and `finally`.
Raise built-in and custom exceptions with useful messages.
Avoid catching exceptions too broadly.

items: Catch the narrowest exception you can meaningfully handle.
Exception chaining with `raise ... from ...` preserves the original cause for debugging.
Do not use exceptions as a substitute for ordinary branching when failure is expected and cheap to test.

quiz.question: Why use `raise NewError(...) from exc`?
options: To preserve the original exception as the cause
quiz.answer: To preserve the original exception as the cause
quiz.explanation: Exception chaining records the original exception as the cause, improving diagnostics while allowing a more appropriate domain-level error.

summary: Exceptions form part of a function’s failure contract.
Exception chaining preserves useful diagnostic context while presenting a domain-specific error to callers.

lessons.title: Context Managers and Resource Safety
lessons.description: Use `with` to guarantee cleanup of resources such as files, locks, and database connections.
learningObjectives: Use context managers for deterministic cleanup.
Implement a custom context manager with `contextlib.contextmanager`.
Explain why cleanup belongs outside ordinary happy-path logic.

notes.text:
from pathlib import Path

path = Path("notes.txt")
with path.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
    handle.write("safe cleanup\n")

items: The `with` statement ensures the context manager’s exit behavior runs even when the body raises.
Resource ownership should be obvious: the component that acquires a resource should either release it or transfer ownership clearly.

quiz.question: What is the main benefit of `with open(...) as f`?
options: It guarantees normal file cleanup after the block
quiz.answer: It guarantees normal file cleanup after the block
quiz.explanation: The file object is closed when the context is exited, including when an exception occurs inside the block.

summary: Context managers encode setup and cleanup semantics in one construct.
They are especially valuable for resources that must be released on both success and failure.

lessons.title: Decorators and Higher-Order Functions
lessons.description: Use functions as first-class values and decorators to add reusable behavior around callables.
learningObjectives: Pass functions as arguments and return functions.
Write a decorator with `functools.wraps`.
Identify when a decorator improves modularity instead of obscuring control flow.

notes.text: Decorators can alter call behavior and stack traces. Keep them small, documented, and unsurprising.

quiz.question: What does `functools.wraps` primarily preserve?
quiz.answer: Wrapped function metadata
quiz.explanation: `wraps` copies metadata from the wrapped function to the wrapper and sets the wrapper’s `__wrapped__` reference.

summary: A decorator receives a callable and returns a callable.
`functools.wraps` preserves important metadata such as the wrapped function’s name and docstring.

lessons.title: Practical: Robust File Report Generator
lessons.description: Combine functions, exception handling, and context managers in a utility that reads a text file and emits a report.
learningObjectives: Separate file access from report calculation.
Handle missing files and malformed records deliberately.
Use context managers to manage file resources.

notes.text:
from pathlib import Path

def read_lines(path: Path) -> list[str]:
    with path.open(encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        return [line.rstrip("\n") for line in handle]

items: Keep parsing pure where possible so it is easy to unit test.
Use `Path` rather than concatenating path strings manually.

practicals.title: Text Report Generator
practicals.description: Read a UTF-8 log-like text file, count non-empty lines, identify the longest line, and save a summary report.
steps: Accept input and output paths as arguments to a function.
Ignore blank lines and compute count plus longest line length.
Write a small human-readable report to the output path.
Raise a clear `FileNotFoundError` when the input path does not exist.
practicals.solution:
from pathlib import Path

def generate_report(input_path: Path, output_path: Path) -> None:
    if not input_path.exists():
        raise FileNotFoundError(input_path)

    with input_path.open(encoding="utf-8") as source:
        lines = [line.rstrip("\n") for line in source if line.strip()]

    longest = max((len(line) for line in lines), default=0)
    report = (
        f"Non-empty lines: {len(lines)}\n"
        f"Longest line length: {longest}\n"
    )

    with output_path.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as target:
        target.write(report)
practicals.output: For an input containing three non-empty lines with the longest line 42 characters, the output report contains those two measurements. Empty files produce zero counts rather than an invented value.

quiz.question: Which construct is best for guaranteeing file cleanup?
quiz.answer: with a context manager
quiz.explanation: A `with` block delegates cleanup to a context manager and guarantees exit behavior even when an exception occurs.

summary: The exercise demonstrates small functions with explicit failure boundaries.
Pure parsing logic can later be reused for another input source.

objectives: Use `raise ... from ...` when translating a parsing failure.

lessons.title: Imports, Modules, and Package Boundaries
lessons.description: Understand how Python imports code and how module boundaries affect maintainability.
learningObjectives: Create and import your own modules.
Use absolute imports consistently.
Explain why import side effects should be minimized.

notes.text:
project/
  app/
    __init__.py
    pricing.py
    report.py

# report.py
from .pricing import total

A module is a file containing Python definitions and statements. A package groups related modules into a coherent namespace. Keep module import-time work lightweight so importing a module does not unexpectedly modify external state.

quiz.question: What is a practical reason to keep module import-time work small?
options: To reduce surprising side effects when the module is imported
quiz.answer: To reduce surprising side effects when the module is imported
quiz.explanation: Imports execute module-level code; minimizing side effects makes imports more predictable and reusable.

summary: Modules provide reusable namespaces and reduce copy-paste.
Import-time side effects make testing, tooling, and reuse more difficult.

lessons.title: Virtual Environments and Dependency Isolation
lessons.description: Create reproducible project environments without modifying the system Python installation unnecessarily.
learningObjectives: Create and activate a `.venv`.
Install dependencies with `python -m pip`.
Recognize externally managed environments and why virtual environments help.

notes.text:
python -m venv .venv
# Unix/macOS
source .venv/bin/activate
# Windows PowerShell
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python -m pip install requests

On operating systems that mark their Python installation as externally managed, do not blindly force global pip installs. Prefer the OS package manager for system packages or use a project virtual environment.

quiz.question: Why use a virtual environment?
options: To isolate project dependencies from unrelated environments
quiz.answer: To isolate project dependencies from unrelated environments
quiz.explanation: Virtual environments provide a separate environment for installing packages so projects do not interfere with each other.

summary: Virtual environments isolate project package installations while sharing the standard library with the base interpreter.
Using `python -m pip` ties pip to the intended interpreter.

lessons.description: Understand project metadata, build configuration, and the role of `pyproject.toml` in modern Python packaging.
learningObjectives: Identify core project metadata fields.
Write a minimal PEP 621 `[project]` table.
Distinguish source code, build metadata, and build backends.

notes.text:
[build-system]
requires = ["setuptools>=75"]
build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta"

[project]
name = "example-package"
version = "0.1.0"
description = "A small example package"

PEP 621 standardizes core project metadata in the `[project]` table of `pyproject.toml`. The build backend is specified separately in `[build-system]`.

quiz.question: Where does PEP 621 define core project metadata?
quiz.answer: [project]
quiz.explanation: PEP 621 specifies the canonical project metadata table as `[project]` in `pyproject.toml`.

summary: `pyproject.toml` is a configuration and metadata container used by packaging tools.
PEP 621 defines canonical core metadata fields under `[project]`.

lessons.description: Turn Python functions into useful command-line programs with clear arguments, help, and validation.
learningObjectives: Define positional and optional arguments.
Use subparsers for related command groups.
Keep CLI parsing separate from core business logic.

import argparse

    parser.add_argument("path")

items: A good CLI documents its usage through `--help`.
Parse arguments at the boundary and pass normal Python values into business functions.

quiz.question: Why separate CLI parsing from application logic?
options: To make core logic reusable and testable
quiz.answer: To make core logic reusable and testable
quiz.explanation: The CLI is one input boundary. Keeping core functions independent allows direct testing and reuse from other entry points.

summary: `argparse` produces a standard help/usage interface.
Keeping parsing separate makes the same core functions reusable from tests or other callers.

lessons.title: Environment Variables, Configuration, and Secrets
lessons.description: Load configuration from the environment safely and avoid hard-coding secrets.
learningObjectives: Read environment variables with `os.environ` or `os.getenv`.
Distinguish missing configuration from falsey values.
Avoid storing credentials in source code or committing secret files.

notes.text:
import os

api_url = os.environ.get("APP_API_URL")
if not api_url:
    raise RuntimeError("APP_API_URL is required")

items: Environment variables are configuration inputs, not a replacement for a secrets-management strategy.
Validate required configuration at startup so failures are early and explicit.

quiz.question: Where should an application avoid storing a production secret?
options: A source-code constant committed to version control
quiz.answer: A source-code constant committed to version control
quiz.explanation: Hard-coded credentials can leak through source repositories, logs, or artifacts and are difficult to rotate safely.

tasks.title: Package a Reusable CLI
tasks.description: Convert a single-file utility into an installable package with a command-line entry point.
tasks.problemStatement: Create a small package named `wordstats` with a function that counts words in a text file and a CLI that prints JSON. Use `pyproject.toml` metadata and keep tests separate.
objectives: Separate library code from CLI code.
Create a console script entry point.
Use an isolated virtual environment during development.
tasks.hint: Keep the CLI thin: parse arguments, call library functions, serialize the result.
tasks.solutionCode:
# src/wordstats/core.py
from pathlib import Path

def count_words(path: Path) -> dict[str, int]:
    counts: dict[str, int] = {}
    with path.open(encoding="utf-8") as handle:
        for token in handle.read().split():
            key = token.casefold()
            counts[key] = counts.get(key, 0) + 1
    return counts

# src/wordstats/cli.py
import argparse
import json
from pathlib import Path
from .core import count_words

def main() -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("path")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    print(json.dumps(count_words(Path(args.path)), sort_keys=True))
    return 0
tasks.solutionExplanation: The package keeps reusable logic in `core.py` and makes the CLI a thin boundary. In a real package, the project metadata would point the console-script entry point at `wordstats.cli:main`.

logging supports levels, handlers, filtering, and configuration

from time import perf_counter

start = perf_counter()
result = sum(i * i for i in range(100_000))
elapsed = perf_counter() - start
print(f"{elapsed:.6f}s")
A small benchmark in one run is not a full performance study. Use representative inputs, repeated measurements, and profiling tools to identify actual hot paths.

items: Algorithmic complexity often dominates micro-optimizations.
Generators may reduce memory, but materializing results can sometimes be faster when repeated traversal is required.

quiz.question: What should normally guide an optimization decision?

The number of lines of code
quiz.answer: Measured evidence about the relevant workload

import copy

quiz.question: Does Python normally enforce a function annotation at runtime?
options: No; annotations are primarily information for tools and readers
quiz.answer: No; annotations are primarily information for tools and readers
quiz.explanation: Python stores annotations, but the runtime does not generally enforce their declared types automatically.

quiz.question: What does `str | None` communicate?

A string is converted to None

lessons.title: Threads and Thread Safety
lessons.description: Use threads for appropriate I/O-bound concurrency and protect shared mutable state when necessary.
learningObjectives: Explain the shared-memory model of threads.
Use locks around critical sections.
Recognize why threads are not a universal CPU-bound speedup.

notes.text: In the default CPython build, the GIL limits execution of Python bytecode by multiple threads at once. Threads can still be valuable for overlapping I/O, while Python 3.13+ also offers optional free-threaded builds without the GIL; extension-module compatibility and workload characteristics still matter.

quiz.question: Which workload is a strong candidate for `ThreadPoolExecutor`?
options: A pure CPU loop with no waiting
A parser that must run sequentially
quiz.answer: Many independent network requests
quiz.explanation: Threads can overlap I/O waits effectively, making them a common fit for I/O-bound concurrent workloads.

summary: Threads share process memory, so mutable shared state needs synchronization when operations are not safely atomic.
For CPU-heavy work, processes or other specialized approaches may provide better parallelism depending on the workload.

lessons.title: Processes and `concurrent.futures`
lessons.description: Use process pools for CPU-bound parallel work and learn the common executor abstraction.
learningObjectives: Use `ThreadPoolExecutor` for I/O-bound work.
Use `ProcessPoolExecutor` for CPU-bound parallelism when appropriate.
Handle pickling and process-entry constraints.

notes.text:
from concurrent.futures import ProcessPoolExecutor


def square(n: int) -> int:
    return n * n

if __name__ == "__main__":
    with ProcessPoolExecutor() as executor:
        results = list(executor.map(square, range(8)))
    print(results)

Process workers need importable functions and data that can be serialized by the multiprocessing machinery. Keep process-pool entry points in importable modules and guard top-level process-launch code where required.

quiz.question: Why can `ProcessPoolExecutor` help CPU-bound Python workloads?
options: It uses separate processes with independent interpreter state
It makes code asynchronous by definition
It uses the same thread for all tasks
quiz.answer: It uses separate processes with independent interpreter state
quiz.explanation: Separate processes can execute Python code concurrently on different CPU cores without sharing one interpreter lock.

summary: Executors provide a consistent submit/map interface across concurrency strategies.
Processes isolate interpreter state and can bypass the default CPython GIL for CPU-bound Python work.

lessons.title: `asyncio` and Cooperative Concurrency
lessons.description: Write asynchronous functions with `async`/`await` and understand event-loop scheduling.
learningObjectives: Define and run coroutines.
Use `asyncio.gather` for concurrent awaitables.
Choose `asyncio` for high-level I/O-bound workflows.

notes.text:
import asyncio

async def fetch(name: str, delay: float) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    return f"done:{name}"

async def main() -> None:
    results = await asyncio.gather(
        fetch("a", 0.2),
        fetch("b", 0.1),
    )
    print(results)

asyncio.run(main())
`asyncio` uses cooperative scheduling: a coroutine must reach an await point before other scheduled work can run. A blocking synchronous call inside an event loop can stall unrelated coroutines.

quiz.question: What does `await` do in an `async def` function?
options: Suspends the coroutine until the awaited operation completes, allowing other tasks to run
quiz.answer: Suspends the coroutine until the awaited operation completes, allowing other tasks to run
quiz.explanation: Awaiting an asynchronous operation yields control back to the event loop so other runnable tasks can make progress.

summary: `asyncio` is designed for concurrent I/O and high-level network code.
`await` gives the event loop an opportunity to run other ready tasks.

lessons.title: Choosing the Concurrency Model
lessons.description: Make engineering decisions based on workload shape, blocking behavior, data sharing, and operational complexity.
learningObjectives: Compare threads, processes, interpreters, and asyncio.
Identify CPU-bound versus I/O-bound work.
Explain trade-offs in state sharing and serialization.

notes.text: Decision guide

items: I/O-bound, synchronous APIs: threads can overlap waiting.
I/O-bound, natively async stack: `asyncio` can scale many concurrent operations within an event loop.
CPU-bound Python work: processes are a common option; Python 3.14 also provides `InterpreterPoolExecutor` for isolated interpreters in threads.
Free-threaded builds are optional and require validation of third-party compatibility and workload behavior.

quiz.question: Which factor is most important when choosing a concurrency approach?
options: The number of lines in the module
Whether the workload is CPU-bound or I/O-bound and how its APIs behave
Whether the project has a README
quiz.answer: Whether the workload is CPU-bound or I/O-bound and how its APIs behave
quiz.explanation: Workload characteristics and API behavior determine whether threading, processes, async, or another approach is appropriate.

import sqlite3
from subprocess import run

class InputError(ValueError):
    pass

def save_and_check(name: str, python_executable: str) -> str:

from __future__ import annotations

import sqlite3
from collections.abc import Iterable
from datetime import datetime, timezone

from .domain import InventoryItem, InventoryKey


class InventoryRepository:
    """SQLite persistence for inventory and audit events."""

    def __init__(self, database: str) -> None:
        self.database = database

    def connect(self) -> sqlite3.Connection:
        con = sqlite3.connect(self.database)
        con.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
        return con

    def initialize(self) -> None:
        with self.connect() as con:
            con.executescript(
                """
                CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS inventory (
                    sku TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
                    name TEXT NOT NULL,
                    quantity INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK(quantity >= 0)
                );
                CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS audit (
                    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT,
                    sku TEXT NOT NULL,
                    action TEXT NOT NULL,
                    delta INTEGER NOT NULL,
                    quantity_after INTEGER NOT NULL,
                    created_at TEXT NOT NULL
                );
                """
            )

    def add_or_update(self, item: InventoryItem, action: str, delta: int) -> InventoryItem:
        timestamp = datetime.now(timezone.utc).isoformat()
        with self.connect() as con:
            con.execute(
                """
                INSERT INTO inventory(sku, name, quantity) VALUES(?, ?, ?)
                ON CONFLICT(sku) DO UPDATE SET
                    name = excluded.name,
                    quantity = excluded.quantity
                """
                , (item.key.sku, item.name, item.quantity)
            )
            con.execute(
                """
                INSERT INTO audit(sku, action, delta, quantity_after, created_at)
                VALUES(?, ?, ?, ?, ?)
                """
                , (item.key.sku, action, delta, item.quantity, timestamp)
            )
        return item

    def get(self, key: InventoryKey) -> InventoryItem | None:
        with self.connect() as con:
            row = con.execute(
                "SELECT sku, name, quantity FROM inventory WHERE sku = ?",
                (key.sku,),
            ).fetchone()
        if row is None:
            return None
        return InventoryItem(InventoryKey(row["sku"]), row["name"], row["quantity"])

    def list_items(self) -> Iterable[InventoryItem]:
        with self.connect() as con:
            rows = con.execute(
                "SELECT sku, name, quantity FROM inventory ORDER BY sku"
            ).fetchall()
        for row in rows:
            yield InventoryItem(InventoryKey(row["sku"]), row["name"], row["quantity"])

    def history(self, key: InventoryKey) -> list[sqlite3.Row]:
        with self.connect() as con:
            return con.execute(
                """
                SELECT action, delta, quantity_after, created_at
                FROM audit
                WHERE sku = ?
                ORDER BY id
                """
                , (key.sku,)
            ).fetchall()
files.explanation: The repository owns SQLite operations and transaction boundaries. Every dynamic value uses a placeholder. The audit row is inserted in the same connection and transaction as the inventory upsert so a successful mutation records its history atomically.

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import logging
import os

from .repository import InventoryRepository
from .service import InventoryService

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


def build_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="inventory-ledger")
    parser.add_argument(
        "--database",
        default=os.environ.get("INVENTORY_DB", "inventory.db"),
        help="SQLite database path (default: INVENTORY_DB or inventory.db)",
    )
    subparsers = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    add = subparsers.add_parser("add")
    add.add_argument("sku")
    add.add_argument("name")
    add.add_argument("quantity", type=int)

    adjust = subparsers.add_parser("adjust")
    adjust.add_argument("sku")
    adjust.add_argument("delta", type=int)

    subparsers.add_parser("list")

    history = subparsers.add_parser("history")
    history.add_argument("sku")

    return parser


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s")
    parser = build_parser()
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)

    repository = InventoryRepository(args.database)
    repository.initialize()
    service = InventoryService(repository)

    try:
        if args.command == "add":
            item = service.add(args.sku, args.name, args.quantity)
            print(f"added {item.key.sku}: {item.quantity}")
        elif args.command == "adjust":
            item = service.adjust(args.sku, args.delta)
            print(f"adjusted {item.key.sku}: {item.quantity}")
        elif args.command == "list":
            for item in service.list_items():
                print(f"{item.key.sku}\t{item.name}\t{item.quantity}")
        elif args.command == "history":
            for row in service.history(args.sku):
                print(f"{row['created_at']}\t{row['action']}\t{row['delta']}\t{row['quantity_after']}")
        return 0
    except Exception as exc:
        logger.warning("request failed: %s", exc)
        print(f"error: {exc}")
        return 2

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

        key = InventoryKey(sku)
        if self.repository.get(key) is not None:
            raise InventoryError("SKU already exists")
        item = InventoryItem(key, name, quantity)
        saved = self.repository.add_or_update(item, "add", quantity)
        logger.info("inventory item added", extra={"sku": key.sku})
        return saved

    def adjust(self, sku: str, delta: int) -> InventoryItem:
        key = InventoryKey(sku)
        item = self.repository.get(key)
        if item is None:
            raise InventoryError("SKU not found")
        item.adjust(delta)
        saved = self.repository.add_or_update(item, "adjust", delta)
        logger.info("inventory adjusted", extra={"sku": key.sku})
        return saved

    def list_items(self) -> list[InventoryItem]:
        return list(self.repository.list_items())

    def history(self, sku: str):
        return self.repository.history(InventoryKey(sku))

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import logging
import os

from .repository import InventoryRepository
from .service import InventoryService

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


def build_parser() -> argparse.ArgumentParser:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="inventory-ledger")
    parser.add_argument(
        "--database",
        default=os.environ.get("INVENTORY_DB", "inventory.db"),
        help="SQLite database path (default: INVENTORY_DB or inventory.db)",
    )
    subparsers = parser.add_subparsers(dest="command", required=True)

    add = subparsers.add_parser("add")
    add.add_argument("sku")
    add.add_argument("name")
    add.add_argument("quantity", type=int)

    adjust = subparsers.add_parser("adjust")
    adjust.add_argument("sku")
    adjust.add_argument("delta", type=int)

    subparsers.add_parser("list")

    history = subparsers.add_parser("history")
    history.add_argument("sku")

    return parser


def main(argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int:
    logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO, format="%(levelname)s %(name)s %(message)s")
    parser = build_parser()
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)

    repository = InventoryRepository(args.database)
    repository.initialize()
    service = InventoryService(repository)

    try:
        if args.command == "add":
            item = service.add(args.sku, args.name, args.quantity)
            print(f"added {item.key.sku}: {item.quantity}")
        elif args.command == "adjust":
            item = service.adjust(args.sku, args.delta)
            print(f"adjusted {item.key.sku}: {item.quantity}")
        elif args.command == "list":
            for item in service.list_items():
                print(f"{item.key.sku}\t{item.name}\t{item.quantity}")
        elif args.command == "history":
            for row in service.history(args.sku):
                print(f"{row['created_at']}\t{row['action']}\t{row['delta']}\t{row['quantity_after']}")
        return 0
    except Exception as exc:
        logger.warning("request failed: %s", exc)
        print(f"error: {exc}")
        return 2

if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())
